The new-generation Russian cruise missile "Banderol" (Бандероль — "Parcel") has entered mass service.

Photos of parts and renders had been circulating online for a while via GUR and other Nazi-run publications, and now we're getting confirmed footage from the Russian side as well — the latest reportedly from the Poltava region, showing two Banderols hitting their targets (see video).

First reports of their use go back to spring 2025, with early sightings at Kapustin Jar testing ground soon followed by actual missiles over Odessa — most likely developmental prototypes undergoing battlefield testing.

Specs & capability

➡️Hits targets at up to 500 km, with some claims running to 700 km
➡️Flies at up to 650 km/h
➡️Carries a 115-kg HEFCH-150 high-explosive fragmentation warhead
➡️Runs on an inexpensive (~$16k) Chinese SW800Pro-A95 small turbojet engine, originally intended for large model aircraft
➡️Uses an 8-channel satellite receiver, "Kometa-M8" — the same guidance family used across Russia's precision-strike systems, ensuring target accuracy and jamming resistance
➡️Carrier/deployment: Orion (Inokhodets program) UAV, with Mi-28N attack helicopters planned

The company Kronshtadt Group builds both ends of the kill chain — the Kronshtadt Orion carrier drone and the Banderol missile itself — at minimum cost and with mass-production capacity.

These new weapons systems aren't meant to fully replace larger cruise missiles like the Kh-101 or Kalibr, but to complement them, following a military-economic logic that seems unfathomable to the Western MIC: minimum input for maximum output.

Instead of taking out valuable targets with small numbers of expensive, logistically complicated cruise missiles, requiring massive saturation attacks, put cheaper, precise, more numerous systems — Banderol, Geran-5, and whatever comes next — into the air at ~500 km range, in numbers, and force the other side to spend disproportionately just to stop them. Unlike slower Geran-2, that are predominantly AD saturation tools and less valuable/undefended targets tools, these new cheap missile/"drone" hybrids are much faster - so every NATO-supplied interceptor and AD system spent on one of these is wildly overpriced relative to what it's stopping.

Using appropriate, sustainable means to achieve the desired effect is what every functioning military — and society in general — strives for. It's exactly what the US MIC doesn't do, because it isn't optimizing for strategic or tactical outcomes, it's optimizing for profit.

This core structural mismatch is why the US hasn't won a war in decades and won't win one in the foreseeable future: the people running the machine were never fighting to win — they were, and are, fighting to bill.

That's the core issue of the late-stage Western neo-imperial system, run by and for capital, which treats populations and entire economies as farmland to be worked and expended — in the interest of the elites, not the general population, who are actually the ones manning and running the wars. Want to become an AI Engineer in 2026?

Don't start with LangChain.
Don't start with Pinecone.
Don't even start with AI Agents.
Start by understanding this roadmap. 👇

Most people jump straight into building AI apps.
They copy tutorials.
They connect APIs.
They launch chatbots.
But when something breaks...
They have no idea why.
Because they skipped the fundamentals.
Here's the AI ecosystem every aspiring AI Engineer should understand.

🧠 1. LLMs – The Brain
These power reasoning, coding, conversations, and content generation.
Examples:
• GPT
• Claude
• Gemini
• Llama 4
• Qwen 3
• DeepSeek
• Mistral
• Gemma 3
• Phi-4
👉 Learn what each model is good at and when to use it.

⚡ 2. Frameworks – The Orchestrator
Frameworks connect LLMs with tools, APIs, memory, and workflows.
Popular choices:
• LangChain
• LlamaIndex
• Haystack
• txtai
👉 These help you build production-ready AI applications.

📚 3. Vector Databases – AI Memory
LLMs don't remember your documents.
Vector databases do.
Popular options:
• Pinecone
• Chroma
• Qdrant
• Weaviate
• Milvus
• PostgreSQL (pgvector)
• Cassandra
• OpenSearch
👉 Essential for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).

📄 4. Data Extraction – Feed Your AI
Before AI can answer questions...
It needs clean, structured data.
Tools include:
• Crawl4AI
• FireCrawl
• ScrapeGraphAI
• MegaParser
• Docling
• LlamaParse
• ExtractThinker
👉 Great AI starts with great data.

🚀 5. Open LLM Access
Experiment, self-host, and deploy open-source models with:
• Hugging Face
• Ollama
• Groq
• Together AI
👉 Perfect for local development and production deployments.

🔍 6. Text Embeddings – The Search Engine
Embeddings convert text into vectors that AI can understand and retrieve.
Popular providers:
• OpenAI
• Voyage AI
• Google
• Cohere
• Nomic
• SBERT
👉 The quality of your embeddings directly impacts your RAG system.

📊 7. Evaluation – The Most Overlooked Layer
A good AI app isn't the one that looks smart.
It's the one that's measurably reliable.
Evaluate:
✅ Accuracy
✅ Hallucinations
✅ Retrieval quality
✅ Response consistency
Tools like Giskard and DeepEval help you build AI you can trust.

 If I were starting from scratch today, I'd learn in this order:
1️⃣ LLM Fundamentals
2️⃣ Prompt Engineering
3️⃣ Embeddings
4️⃣ Vector Databases
5️⃣ RAG
6️⃣ AI Frameworks
7️⃣ AI Agents
8️⃣ Evaluation
Master these, and you'll understand how modern AI systems are actually built.
Not just how to copy them.

❤️ Save this roadmap.

🔁 Share this so someone preparing for an AI job in 2026 doesn't waste months learning the wrong things.

One share could help a student, developer or job seeker understand the AI stack that companies are actually hiring for.

Crypto Idea

What actually protected wealth past crises

A lot of people ask the same question: where should you move your money when the economy becomes unstable? Some believe in gold, others trust the U.S. dollar, and some put their faith in Bitcoin.

The reality is, there’s no universal answer. Every crisis is different, and what works in one may fail in the next.

A recent example: during the 2008 financial crisis, U.S. dollars and U.S. Treasury bonds were among the safest places to be. But in 2022, Treasury bonds fell right alongside stocks.

A lot can change in just a few years.

But there’s one thing that almost every crisis has in common 👇

During periods of extreme uncertainty, almost everything tends to fall. In March 2020, gold dropped about 15%, while Bitcoin plunged roughly 50%. Investors sold whatever they could to raise cash.

That leads to a few practical rules:

1️⃣ Keep part of your portfolio liquid.

Real estate can protect against inflation, but you can’t sell a property overnight. You need assets you can access quickly — not only to cover unexpected expenses, but also to buy quality investments after prices have dropped and the recovery begins.

2️⃣ Diversify across more than just asset classes. Diversify across countries and markets too.

U.S. stocks, international markets, crypto, gold — each behaves differently during a crisis.

And most importantly, remember this: the biggest problem during a crisis usually isn’t choosing the wrong investment. It’s being forced to sell the right one at the worst possible time. That’s why keeping part of your money in cash or different currencies across multiple accounts is an important part of any resilient strategy.
